newsitem.title: USA: Derivatives group rejects proposed accounting rule.
newsitem.headline: Derivatives group rejects proposed accounting rule.

text.p: International Swaps and Derivatives Association said on Wednesday it would oppose proposed accounting rules that would force companies to carry all derivatives on their balance sheets.
Financial Accounting Standards Board proposed the change for off-balance sheet financial instruments in a June exposure draft that would also limit the use of hedge accounting.

"Although we are sympathetic to the FASB's desire to clarify certain anomalies that currently exist in the accounting framework, the FASB's proposed approach is not an improvement," Gay Evans, chairman of the group, said.

Evans, also senior managing director at Bankers Trust International, told reporters at a press briefing here that the FASB proposal would increase the volatility of earnings of companies using derivatives without providing much useful information.

And that may deter companies from using derivatives even to reduce risk, she said. "It may instead lead companies to take on more risk rather than reduce risk through appropriate use of risk management instruments," Evans said.
The derivatives group filed on Monday a 25-page comment letter laying out its objections with the accounting board.
At the most basic level, each use of a derivative should be accounted for in the same manner as the business activity it is part of, Evans said.
For example, companies often sell floating rate bonds and swap to a fixed rate and save five or 10 basis points over just selling fixed rate bonds.

Under the FASB proposal, the swap would not qualify as a hedge for accounting purposes so changes in its value would be reflected on the balance sheet, but changes in the value of the bond would not be recorded.
The derivatives group also said Wednesday it had changed its by-laws to formally include a focus on risk management activities.
"Financial risk management is increasingly what ISDA is all about," Evans said. "This is a natural evolution and reflects changes that are going on in the industry."
The group had already been addressing technical and regulatory aspects of risk management for several years.
